title: Why the Lobster calls into the agent runtime instead of running the agent itself
dek: The bookmark pipeline taught us a non-obvious lesson: the workflow engine should hand work to the agent at a clean handoff, not try to be the agent.
body:
The first version of the bookmark pipeline was the obvious one. The Lobster — our workflow engine — would take a batch of bookmarks, run curation, generate specs, post approvals, and create tasks. End to end, in one runner.

It worked for about a week.

The problem wasn't that the Lobster was slow or unreliable. The problem was that it didn't have enough context. Curation needs the weekly review, the spec templates, the prior bookmarks that got accepted and rejected, the live tasks queue, and the personal notes that explain *why* something matters. Spec generation needs the codebases it's targeting, the design system, and the existing tasks. None of that lives in the Lobster. None of it should. The Lobster's job is to be a deterministic, resumable, idempotent state machine. Loading it up with project context is exactly the wrong shape.

So we did the thing that felt wrong at the time: we moved the intelligent work *out* of the Lobster and into the agent runtime.

## The handoff

The Lobster is now responsible for one thing: advancing a bookmark from one well-defined state to the next. It is idempotent, so a re-run does the same thing. It leaves bookmarks that need context — curation, spec authoring — in states like `curation` or `spec_needed`. It does not try to be the curator or the spec author.

Heartbeat is what does the intelligent work. Heartbeat reads the bookmark state, loads the context the agent runtime already has, performs the curation or the spec request, and writes the result back. After the task is performed, heartbeat moves the bookmark to the next state. The next Lobster run picks it up and progresses the pipeline.

This split was the unlock. The Lobster is good at being a state machine. The agent is good at having context. Neither is good at doing the other's job. Forcing them to share a runtime was where the previous version broke.

## Why not just call the agent from the Lobster?

We considered it. Lobster is a workflow engine — it can shell out, it can make HTTP calls, it can do anything a script can. We could have given it a wrapper that calls the agent runtime directly. We even prototyped it.

The problem with that approach is that the Lobster is supposed to be resumable. It keeps a resume token between runs so it can pick up exactly where it left off after a crash, a deploy, or a manual stop. The moment you put an LLM call inside that loop, the resume token becomes a hostage: the LLM call might take 30 seconds or 30 minutes, the context window is finite, the cost is non-zero, and a re-run re-pays all of it. For a batch-style workflow like the bookmark pipeline, that is unacceptable. We had real cases where the Lobster ran twice on the same batch and paid for the same spec generation twice.

The fix was the state-machine split. The Lobster's only state transitions are the cheap, deterministic ones. The expensive, context-heavy work is owned by heartbeat, which has its own cost visibility, its own rate control, and its own failure handling. If the LLM call fails, heartbeat retries it on the next cycle. The Lobster doesn't care. The resume token is intact.

## The constraint that came out of it

The bookmark pipeline works on batches, not one-run-per-task like the content factory. A batch of bookmarks enters the pipeline together, advances through the same states together, and the Lobster can only run one spec request at a time per batch. That's a real constraint, and it falls out of the design: if the Lobster advanced one bookmark at a time, the LLM cost and latency would be paid per bookmark instead of per batch, and the resume token would be tied to a single LLM call instead of a deterministic state transition. The batch shape is what keeps the system fast and resumable.

For the code factory, the calculus is different. Each task is its own PR, its own review thread, its own approval path. The Lobster runs once per task, checks the transition conditions, and scripts anything that's scriptable. The intelligent work — the design call, the implementation shape, the test strategy — is still agent work, but it lives in PR-driven approvals, not in the Lobster's resume token. The Lobster checks the PR state, advances the task, and waits. The PR is the resume mechanism.

## What I'd tell someone designing the same thing

Don't try to make the workflow engine smart. The minute you put an LLM call inside a resumable loop, you lose the property that made the workflow engine worth having. Move the intelligent work to the place that already has context — the agent runtime, the heartbeat, wherever your system already accumulates the long tail of operational knowledge. Keep the workflow engine boring. Boring is a feature, not a limitation.

The split we landed on is: Lobster advances state, agents perform work, heartbeat glues them together. The handoff is a status change in a database, not a function call. That's what makes the system survivable across crashes, deploys, and the inevitable moments when the LLM call returns something the workflow engine didn't expect.

If you're building something similar, the question to ask isn't 'how do I make my workflow engine smarter'. It's 'what is the smallest possible state transition I can make resumable'. Do that one well, and the rest follows.
